search.title: Forecasting the Next Patient Event with Next-Token Pretraining

sections.heading: The problem: a patient history is a long, irregular timeline
sections.body: A patient's history is not a neat table. It is a long, irregular timeline: diagnoses, prescriptions and procedures, scattered across years, with gaps of days or months between events. Traditional models flatten this timeline into hand-built features, counts and recency flags, and in doing so they discard the order and timing of events, which carry most of the signal. The question this model answers is simple: can we read the whole history as it happened, and forecast what comes next?

figures.alt: From claims to tokens: a patient's diagnoses, prescriptions and procedures on a timeline, each mapped to a token id, forming one sequence of the last 2,048 tokens
figures.caption: From claims to tokens

sections.heading: The model: claims become tokens, the model reads them in order
sections.body: Every claim becomes one token from the OMOP standard vocabulary: a diagnosis, a prescription, a procedure, each with its own id. A patient's history becomes a sequence of tokens, the most recent 2,048 of them. Each token is embedded with a frozen MedRep table, 768 dimensions per code, so codes that mean similar things sit close together, then a linear adapter projects it to 512 dimensions. Time gets its own embedding: the gap since each event is bucketed into 11 bins, from 1 day to 1,460 days, so each event carries both what it was and how long ago it occurred. Twelve identical blocks read the sequence left to right; a Mamba mixer carries information forward from earlier events, updating its memory as it reads, and SwiGLU reworks what was read at each position. The last real position, plus the patient's age, becomes one patient vector, and three heads produce three different predictions from it: a binary head for will it happen, a discrete-hazard head for when, and a count head for how many.

figures.alt: One forward pass: token ids and day deltas flow through a frozen MedRep embedding and a log-time embedding, a linear adapter to 512 dimensions, 12 pre-norm residual blocks with Mamba mixer and SwiGLU, then pooling of the last real position plus age into three heads
figures.caption: One forward pass

sections.heading: Pretrain once, then finetune and calibrate per outcome
sections.body: The backbone is pretrained once, by next-token prediction on millions of patient histories: predict the next event, and in doing so learn the patterns of how diseases and treatments progress. Each outcome then gets its own head and its own finetune, with the whole backbone tuned together. A raw score is not a probability, so every head is calibrated with isotonic regression before it ships, and patients are rolled up to the HCP level for the field. Nothing reaches production on a metric alone: each candidate is gated, scored on AUC, calibration and precision at k, and a human promotes the challenger to production. One backbone serves many forecasts, and every reported probability is calibrated.

figures.alt: Pretrain once, then finetune and calibrate per outcome: pretrain by next-token prediction, finetune per head, calibrate with forward isotonic, gate and evaluate, human promotes to production; patient probabilities roll up to HCP scores and a field priority list
figures.caption: Pretrain once, then finetune and calibrate per outcome

ads.title: Recommender Algorithms in Pharma: Bringing MMoE into Next-Best-Action

sections.heading: The problem: budget goes to the wrong customers
sections.body: Most targeting models rank customers by how likely they are to buy. The problem: the top of that list is full of people who would buy anyway. Budget goes to customers who convert with or without our outreach, instead of customers whose decision our message can actually change. Ranking by conversion probability cannot tell the two apart, so much of the spend has no incremental effect.

figures.alt: Funnel from email sent to new prescription, with the signal fading at each step
figures.caption: Signal fades and noise grows as we move away from the email.

sections.heading: The model: one MMoE, four tasks
sections.body: Instead of one model per goal, we built a single model that predicts four things at once: new prescriptions, rep visits, clicks, and opt-outs. Four small expert networks do the work, and each goal has its own gate that controls which experts it uses. The goals share experts where they behave alike and stay separate where they do not. The dense signals, clicks and visits, also help the model learn about new prescriptions, which are far too rare to learn on their own.

figures.alt: MMoE model architecture: customer features and treatment feed a shared tower, four experts, four per-task gates and four task heads
figures.caption: MMoE inside an S-Learner uplift frame: one model, four tasks.

sections.heading: Why it works: each task gets its own gate
sections.body: When several goals share one network, they interfere with each other: improving one goal can make another worse. Per-task gates fix this. The gates learn from the data how much to share: goals with similar patterns share experts, goals with conflicting patterns use different ones. The same gate can route two different customers to different experts, because the right mix depends on the customer and the content.

figures.alt: Shared-bottom gradient conflict: two task gradients pull the shared parameters in different directions, with gradient-direction and seesaw panels
figures.caption: When gradients conflict, the shared update can point uphill for one task.

figures.alt: Gate routing for two customer-content pairs: the same NBRx gate weights experts differently for an existing user and a non-user
figures.caption: Same gate, different row, different weights: Case A leans on Expert 1, Case B on Expert 3.

recsys.title: Field Engagement, Ranked by Effect: R-Learner Uplift for Rep Prioritization

sections.heading: The problem: visits go to the wrong HCPs
sections.body: Most field plans rank HCPs by how likely they are to prescribe and send reps to the top of the list. The problem: the top of that list is full of people who would prescribe anyway, people who convert with or without a visit. Rep time goes to them instead of the HCPs whose decision a visit can actually change. Ranking by prescribing probability cannot tell the two apart, so much of the field budget has no incremental effect.

figures.alt: Why R-learner wins when targeting is selective: visited HCPs cluster at high baseline propensity and not-visited HCPs at low, with only a thin overlap; residualization isolates the surprise visits
figures.caption: Why R-learner wins when targeting is selective

sections.heading: The model: R-learner estimates the effect directly
sections.body: Instead of the S-learner, one model that predicts the outcome and takes a difference, R-learner works in two stages. Stage 1 fits two models: m(x), how much this HCP prescribes, and e(x), how likely this HCP is to be visited. Stage 2 fits the effect on the residuals, through the R-loss: the outcome residual (Y - m(x)) against the treatment residual (t - e(x)). Those residuals are the quasi-random variation, visits the targeting rule did not predict, so the effect it learns is the visit’s own effect, not the HCP’s baseline.

figures.alt: S-learner versus R-learner: one model that takes a difference, against a two-stage R-learner that fits the effect on residualized outcome and treatment
figures.caption: Field engagement · S-learner vs R-learner

sections.heading: From the effect to a priority list
sections.body: Each HCP gets one number: τ̂(x), the incremental NBRx a visit is expected to add. Rank HCPs by τ̂, highest first, and fill rep capacity in that order; the rest get no visit, or digital only. The top of this list looks different from the old one: not the biggest prescribers, but the HCPs whose decision a visit can change. A visit is worth making when the expected incremental NBRx is worth more than the visit costs.

figures.alt: From tau-hat to a field priority list: HCPs ranked by incremental NBRx, rep capacity filled in that order, the rest no visit or digital only
figures.caption: From τ̂ to a field priority list

mlops.title: Marketing Mix at Two Levels: A Sequential Model, Checked by PSM / DiD

sections.heading: Two levels of campaigns
sections.body: Campaigns run at two levels. Customer-level campaigns target individual HCPs, at the grain of HCP and week: what each HCP saw, each week. DMA-level campaigns broadcast to a whole market, at the grain of DMA and week: what each DMA saw, each week. Each HCP is in exactly one DMA, so DMA exposure is shared by every HCP in that market. The outcome is the same at both grains: HCP-week NBRx.

figures.alt: Campaigns live at two levels: customer-level campaigns target individual HCPs at HCP-week grain, DMA-level campaigns broadcast to a whole market at DMA-week grain; DMA exposure is shared by every HCP in that market
figures.caption: Campaigns live at two levels

sections.heading: The model: sequential, customer first, DMA second
sections.body: Stage 1 builds an HCP-week linear model from the customer-level campaign, with adstock, and HCP attributes. It predicts HCP-week NBRx, and what it cannot explain becomes the residual. Stage 2 fits that residual with the DMA-level campaign, with adstock, and DMA attributes, keeping only the terms that explain the residual, stepwise. While both stages run, the adstock of both campaigns is searched: try decay and half-life values, refit, pick the best. The order matters: DMA campaigns are shared across HCPs in a market, so they belong in the second stage, after the HCP-level signal is accounted for.

figures.alt: Sequential two-stage model: stage 1 fits an HCP-week linear model from the customer-level campaign and HCP attributes, stage 2 fits the residual with the DMA-level campaign and DMA attributes with stepwise selection, while the adstock of both campaigns is searched
figures.caption: Sequential model - customer first, DMA second

sections.heading: Measure what already ran: a reusable PSM / DiD framework
sections.body: For each past campaign, first match treated HCPs and DMAs to untreated look-alikes on observables: same baseline, same market, same history. Then compare before against after, treated against matched control: the campaign's effect, net of trends. Per channel, estimate the lag effect, how long the effect lasts after the campaign ends, and build a reasonable adstock interval per channel. That interval feeds the adstock search in the sequential model. The framework is reusable: run the same steps on every past campaign and keep the lag estimates up to date.

figures.alt: Reusable PSM / DiD framework: match treated HCPs and DMAs to untreated look-alikes, compare before vs after against the matched control, estimate each channel's lag effect and build an adstock interval that feeds the adstock search
figures.caption: Measure what already ran - PSM / DiD

jobs.role: Senior Machine Learning Engineer, AI Predictive Solutions
bullets: Contributed to prototyping and scaling ML systems for customer engagement prediction and promotional content personalization; staged rollout showed stronger performance than existing organic and event-driven strategies, supporting deployment across the U.S. portfolio and $9M in annual marketing spend.

Field Engagement Recommendation: Participated in developing uplift modeling framework to estimate the effect of field reach on customers' conversion and usage frequency, built regional optimization algorithms with feedback loop to automate weekly field engagement recommendations; scaled the solution to 6 product lines with development tailored to each product's market landscape and sales structure.

Model Evaluation Framework: Designed the model evaluation framework for the orchestration system, combining time-based offline validation, uplift evaluation (Qini/AUUC), and calibration checks with online holdout and A/B testing, using opt-outs as a guardrail metric to support model release decisions.

Digital Engagement Orchestration: Architected the next-generation digital orchestration system, decoupling channel delivery from uplift modeling and leveraging a shared-bottom multi-task DCN-v2 framework; integrated multi-funnel objectives (clicks/opens, site engagement, and rep follow-up success) to enable robust upper-funnel estimation and facilitate content selection.

Content Exploration & Cold-Start Solution: In support of the AI Content Hub, designed SBERT subject-line embeddings, ID embeddings, and a Thompson sampling bandit framework to address cold start problems and enable exploration of new content, allowing new content to be tested and activated efficiently within the existing digital orchestration system.

MLOps & Infra: Collaborated with the AI Infra team to continuously improve repo tooling: introduced Dagster for pipeline orchestration, Databricks MLflow for experiment tracking, and Lakehouse Monitoring, while enhancing unit and integration test robustness. Established repo-level agent usage guidelines and Skills following enterprise Claude adoption.

Developed in-house causal inference toolkits for customer- and geo-level campaign efficacy measurement. The toolkit supported six H2 2023 analyses and remains in use and is maintained by the team, reducing reliance on external vendors.

Standardized customer-level campaign evaluation with config-driven propensity-score matching and inverse-propensity weighting workflows that support multiple modeling algorithms for propensity scoring and automated statistical validation of covariate balance between test and control groups.

Automated geo-level campaign measurement that takes a campaign window and DMA list as input and outputs difference-in-differences and synthetic control estimates with pre-period fit diagnostics and plots.

Supported development of Experience Engine, an ML system that predicts member disengagement risk and content affinity; conducted feature selection and model benchmarking to inform final model selection.
